title: WebSockets vs Polling vs Server Sent Events
content:
2. Starting From Basics — Server and Client

Whenever we talk about any application, any SaaS, or anything in computer science — what do you have?

You have a server, of course.

Because there is a server, whoever uses this server, whoever makes requests to the server — what do we call them? We call them clients.

A client is nothing but just a user — a computer, a laptop, a user.


3. Request-Response Cycle

Here, the request-response cycle is completed. This is called the request-response cycle:

Client initiates a request. Server processes the request and sends back a response, and the request-response cycle is complete.

4. Problem With Request-Response

But here comes a problem.

If you have completed one request-response cycle, that means the server cannot send data again to the client.

connection is close ; 

Let's take an example.

5. Stock Market Example

  • A stock market server stores all the stock data and can handle many requests.
  • Multiple clients request the current stock market data from the server.
  • The server responds to each client, completing the request-response cycle, so every client gets the latest data.

    • 6. The Real Problem

    Now what happens is:

    someone sold something , price are fluctuating 

    So let's say this one sold something, or this one bought something. It got new data.

    So now what happened is: as soon as the request-response was completed, the data changed. Data has changed on our backend.

    That means for this client, and this client, and this client — the data they now have has become stale.

    What does stale mean?

    That data is no longer fresh. Data has changed on the server, but our client still has stale data.

    Which is not a good thing.

    7. Why Real-Time Systems Are Needed

    That is where your real-time-ness comes in.

    That is where you will face this problem: how does the server tell your client that some data has changed?

    Now I know here a lot of people will judge, a lot of answers will say, "We will use WebSocket."

    That is the real problem — because WebSockets are marketed a lot, and everyone knows about WebSocket.


    8. First Solution — WebSockets

    The first solution, which you had already guessed, is WebSockets.

    9. How WebSockets Work

    In WebSocket, what happens is: you create a stateful connection.

    Now what will happen is this client will say, "I want to make a connection with you." There is an upgrade request that we have already discussed in our WebSocket video.

    So this particular connection will never close. It will always remain open.

    It's a fully duplex connection.

    So what happens here is: when you make a WebSocket connection, you tell your server, "This is my request, please upgrade it into something known as WebSocket" — meaning fully duplex.

    Then what happens is the server does not close that connection. The client also does not close that connection.

    And this is where you have a full duplex connection.



    That means what will happen in this particular scenario: if this client sent any update, this server can pass that information to all its clients that "update your data, update your data."

    So that means it's a full duplex connection.

    14. Advantages of WebSockets

    We understood that WebSocket is a very good connection. It's full duplex. Of course, server can send data anytime. Client can send data anytime.

    • Full duplex communication
    • Server can send data anytime
    • Client can send data anytime
    • Real-time updates

    15. Problems With WebSockets

    But what are the downsides of this?

    The downside is that scaling WebSockets is very difficult because it is a stateful connection.

    Can a million clients make a full connection with this one server? Obviously it depends on how big that server is.

    That means here you cannot do horizontal scaling easily. You always have to upgrade the server.

    If you have 1 million clients, and one day if it becomes 2 million, you have to upgrade your server because it's a stateful connection. This is not a stateless connection.

    And it's very difficult to scale — that is the main problem.


    17. Additional Complexity of creating one more layer

    So you basically have to build one more layer, where these servers can also communicate among themselves.

    So usually it's very difficult to scale WebSockets on a large system.

    This is the main problem that comes with a fully duplex system.

    18. Important Question

    But one thing I want to tell you — if we go back to our example: do we really need a full duplex system? 

    So the answer is kind of no.

    pull hi toh kr rhe h , push toh bhot km horha h toh yeh bhot bda overkill rhega ki lgatar state wala connection banana 

    So here, using WebSockets would be a bit of an overkill.

    19. Second Solution — Polling

    So let's move on to the second thing — what can we use here? We can actually use something like Polling.

    Polling means: ask the server again and again. "Hey, has any update come? Hey, has any update come? Hey, has any update come?" 

    So what you can do is: you can basically set an interval here. Let's say I can set an interval of 2 seconds — every 2 seconds, go and ask the server for an update.

    21. Stale Time

    That means what is your stale time? 2 seconds.

    22. Common Doubt

    I know here a question will come — , I like WebSocket more than this. Here we are bothering the server again and again."

    We are bombarding the server with multiple requests.

    Right? We are asking, "did something come? No. Did something come? No."

    23. Why Polling Can Be Better

    But the reality is: this is a much better approach. I will tell you why.

    I told you that in reality, you don't have just one server. Yes and no — in reality you have a lot of servers.

    And all these servers sit behind a Load Balancer.

    So let's say this is your... this is your Load Balancer.

    If this server gets destroyed, if this server gets destroyed, your connection will break. That connection will break.

    25. Polling Advantage

    But what will happen here? Because you are polling, you are always opening a new connection. but humara server ek hi h vetic me 

    So what is basically happening here is: when you poll, your request does not go to the same server. Of course, that's the work of the Load Balancer.

    So your requests keep getting load balanced across multiple servers.

    That means if you are making a lot of requests, you are not really bombarding one server. That's okay. You will always go to a different server.

    26. Fault Tolerance

    So if this server goes down while polling, that's okay, right? My next request will not go to it. My next request may go to this one instead.

    So you always have a chance that you will always get a successful response. And you are not dependent on any one server.

    27. Horizontal Scaling

    What can I do? I can add more servers. Here — if I feel that load is increasing on my servers, I can add more servers.

    So that's fine. More clients — sometimes the request went to this one, sometimes it went to this one.

    28. Polling Summary

    So in polling, what happens is: the client is responsible for asking again and again that "I need fresh data."

    So your stock market — your stock market application — usually you poll in it. So you can have a polling time of, let's say, 1 second, and even 2 seconds.

    So every 2 seconds your client will ask, "I need fresh data, I need fresh data, I need fresh data."

    What does this give us? We can maintain a stateless connection with the server, which is always a scalable approach.

    29. Types of Polling

    Now within polling too, you have two kinds of polling. You have something known as Short Polling and you have something known as Long Polling.

    30. Long Polling

    First let's talk about Long Polling first.)

    The server will hold your request for a while. It will say, "since a lot of updates can happen, let me give all the updates in one go."

    So the server held your request. Held it for, let's say, 5 seconds.


    And this continues — this is called Long Polling.

    Because what is the server doing? It holds your request for a long time. So it will give you, in that duration of 5 seconds, whatever is updating, in one go.

    This reduces the number of requests to the server.

    31. Long Polling Flow

    But how many requests did I make? Only two.

    So within two requests, I can bring 10 seconds worth of updates.

    This is Long Polling.

     five requests.

    32. Benefit of Long Polling

    So Long Polling — if we read here — you can see: Long polling is a variation of traditional polling technique where the server holds the client request open until new data is available.

    So, upon receiving new data, the server responds and closes the connection. The client then immediately sends another request, creating a near-continuous connection.

    So here basically what happens is — here I took the 5 seconds example. But the server can also hold it just until new data is available.

    You sent a request. Let's assume no update came at all — then hold its request. As soon as new data came, send it.

    So basically what happens here: it's a near-continuous connection.


    PollingClient: "Har 5 sec mein batao update hai?"
    Long PollingClient: "Bata dena jab update aaye."
    WebSocketEk connection continuously open rehta hai, dono sides messages bhej sakti hai

    33. Official Explanation

    Long Polling: Server keeps the request open until new data becomes available. When new data arrives: Respond, close connection. Client immediately sends a new request. Creates a near-continuous connection.

    34. Advantages of Long Polling

    Now features are of course:

    • Reduced latency
    • Server-triggered responses
    • Efficient for real-time cases

    35. Long Polling Problem

    But there is a problem here.

    The problem is: again, a server has a limitation on how many connections it can keep open.

    That is the main problem.

    If 10,000 clients got connected with this particular server, and there is no update for the next 1 minute — let's assume by chance no update came — then it will keep 10,000 connections open, which is not an optimal thing.

    So that is the main thing. But this particular process is called Long Polling.

    So in Long Polling, what happens is your server holds back the connection.

    37. Short Polling Flow

    Short polling, as the name says — what does the client do? Client will send a request. Server will respond back to it on the spot.

    Now what you can do is: server client will say, "okay I just got data now. No update came. Let me wait a little." So the server thought — sorry, the client thought — "let's do one thing, let's wait for 2 seconds. And then make a request again."

    Server will respond back right away. Then the client will think, "okay, let's wait 2 seconds." Then a request will come again. Then it will get data again, if any is available.

    So here you can see what is happening — the waiting is being decided by the client, which is what we were doing here.

    So this is basically known as Short Polling.

    38. Key Difference

    • Long Polling: Server decides the waiting.
    • Short Polling: Client decides the waiting.

    39. Official Explanation

    jb merko pkaa pta h ki data kb change hoga

    So here you have Short Polling — involves the client sending HTTP requests at regular intervals to check for updates.

    So here the client basically sends at regular intervals. The server processes each request and returns the response immediately, regardless of whether new data is available or not.

    40. Downside of Short Polling

    The only problem here is: the number of requests becomes quite large.

    So that's the only downside.

    41. Advantage of Short Polling

    But here, your server doesn't need to hold back any response. So we can keep the server free immediately.

    42. Short Polling Use Cases

    So if you see its use case, its use cases are: periodic data updates, useful for data that changes quickly.

    • We use this in health checks.
    • We use this in content feeds.

    So usually, when should you do Short Polling? When you know that data will be constantly changing.

    In the stock market, I know that every 2 seconds, or every 5 seconds, there is going to be fresh data available. So there I should do Short Polling.

    43. Chat System Example

    But in a chat system, I don't know. Maybe the other person didn't reply to me at all.

    So there we can even use Long Polling, or there you can also use WebSockets.

    44. Third Solution — Server Sent Events (SSE)

    There is something known as SSE. It stands for Server Sent Events.

    As the name says, the server keeps sending you events.

    45. Difference From WebSocket

    This is a little like WebSocket, but it is not duplex. It's single-sided.

    46. SSE Flow

    Your client says, "hey, make a connection." So your client said, "hey, make a connection with me, and keep this connection open."

    47. What Happens Next?

    So what can happen: any update came, server will respond to you. But this connection will still not be closed.

    But the client cannot send data. This is one way. Here, this thing is not possible. This is not possible. Client cannot send data.

    The connection is open. This server can keep sending you some data. The server can keep sending you some data.

    So whenever an update comes on the server, it will send you data. That is why this is called Server Sent Events.

    And if you want to close the connection, of course you can close the connection. And then you will have to make a connection again. Then again your server will keep sending you data.

    This is known as Server Sent Events.

    48. Important Limitation

    Client cannot send data through this connection.

    Only:

    • Server → Client is possible.
    • Client → Server is not possible.

    49. SSE Characteristics

    • One-way communication
    • Long-lived HTTP connection
    • Server continuously pushes updates
    • Client only receives

    50. Definition Mentioned

    Server Sent Events: A web technology that enables a server to push real-time, unidirectional updates to a client, typically a web browser, over a single long-lived HTTP connection.

    51. Final Comparison

    WebSockets

    • Full duplex
    • Client ↔ Server
    • Harder to scale

    Polling

    • Client repeatedly asks for updates
    • Stateless
    • Scalable

    Long Polling

    • Server holds request
    • Fewer requests
    • Open connections remain

    Short Polling

    • Immediate response
    • More requests
    • Server freed immediately

    Server Sent Events (SSE)

    • One-way
    • Server → Client only
    • Long-lived connection

    52. Final Conclusion

    So every mechanism has its own use case, its own drawbacks, its own pros and cons.

    So based on the application that you are building, you have to choose which mechanism is best fit for your particular use case.

    You should know the trade-offs. You should know what are the cons, what are the pros, and what you are building.

    So whatever application you are building — how much predictability is there in it, how much rapid data change happens, how much is your scale, how much is your budget, what kind of application, how much real-time-ness you want — based on that, either you will use WebSocket, or you will use Server Sent Events, and you will choose Polling, in which you have Short Polling and Long Polling.

    This was a video on all the real-time protocols, or real-time-ness — how you can build a real-time application. It was more of a diagrammatic video.
